It is as if he perceives things with his eyes through true reason, and by the confidence of his belief, he stands out among men as much as the sun outshines the other stars with its light. For the sun itself illuminates the other stars not so much by the greatness of its power as by its divinity and holiness. Believe that this is the second god, O Asclepius, who governs the rest and illuminates all worldly beings, whether they possess a soul or are inanimate. 

For if the world is a living being <note>original: "animal mundus," referring to the Platonic and Stoic concept of the Anima Mundi or World Soul</note> that is always alive, and was, and is, and shall be, then nothing in the world is mortal. For since every single part is living, and exists within the world itself as within one and the same ever-living being, there is no place for mortality. Therefore, God himself must be most full of life and eternity, if it is necessary for him to live forever. 

Thus the sun, just like the world, is everlasting; so too is he forever the governor of living things, or rather the provider and dispenser of their total vitality. God, therefore, is the everlasting governor of the living beings, or the vital things that are in the world, and the eternal dispenser of life itself. He dispensed life to all vital beings once and for all by an eternal law, according to this manner which I shall describe.

<summary>Hermes explains that a pious man excels others like the sun among stars and defines the world as an eternally living being governed by the sun as a second god. He asserts that because the world is a living whole, nothing within it is truly mortal, as life is dispensed by eternal law.</summary>
<keywords>piety, sun, Asclepius, World Soul, immortality, divine governance, vital spirit, eternal law</keywords>
